info.title: Bill Analysis Front Service
info.description:
API actions for running analytics queries on vendor bill data managed in Cloud Cost Optimization. For information on connecting cloud bill data to Cloud Cost Optimization, see the [Getting Started guide](https://docs.flexera.com/flexera/EN/Optima/GettingStarted.htm).


The API is available at the following endpoints:
* (NAM) https://api.optima.flexeraeng.com/bill-analysis
* (EU) https://api.optima-eu.flexeraeng.com/bill-analysis
* (APAC) https://api.optima-apac.flexeraeng.com/bill-analysis

## Auth
Requests made to the API must be authenticated using a token obtained from the [Cloud Management API](http://docs.rightscale.com/api/general_usage.html#authentication).
For some APIs, an "Api-Version" header must also be set; the current version is "1.0".

## Required Roles
Requests to the Costs resource requires that the user have one or more of the following roles on an Org or BillingCenter (or parent BillingCenter of a child BillingCenter):
  * Cloud Management: "enterprise_manager", "billing_center_admin", or "billing_center_viewer"
  * Flexera One: "Manage organization", "Manage cloud", "Manage billing centers", or "View cloud costs"


# Adjustment Definition API

This API allows you to define adjustments to be applied to all cost data in the org.
This enables use cases like markup and markdown, by specifying rules to determine what percentages should be used.

An example adjustment:
  * Name: **IT Dept Markup**
  * Rules:
        * if vendor = AWS: **20%**
        * if vendor = GCP: **10%**
      
This would markup AWS costs by 20% by adding an "IT Dept Markup" adjustment row for each matching cost row, containing 20% of the original cost value. And a similar 10% markup for GCP costs. And any other costs not matching those rules would be unaffected.

The adjustment's rules are evaluated in order, stopping when the first rule matches, and that determines the percentage.

You can define multiple adjustments in a list. They may even build on one another if the costs need to compound on one another.

You can have the adjustment list change over time by specifying a new list to be used as of a given effective date (year-month).
A list will remain in effect until the effective date of the next list. So for any given date, only one list would apply.

# Budget API

## Deprecated
~~~~
This API is deprecated and is no longer being maintained. Please refer to new API documentation found below
~~~~
https://developer.flexera.com/docs/api/finops-analytics/v1


The Budget API allows you to create, read, update, and delete budgets, as well as generate budget reports to compare your planned budget with actual spend. Budgets are defined using a combination of dimensions, year-months, and segments to provide a flexible and detailed breakdown of your costs.

A budget is defined with the following properties:

- `name`: A descriptive name to uniquely identify the budget.
- `metric`: The cost metric used for the budget, such as `cost_amortized_unblended_adj`.
- `dimensions`: An array of dimensions used for budget breakdown, such as `vendor_account`, or `rbd_team`.
- `yearMonths`: An array of year-month strings like "2023-01", defining the time period covered by the budget.
- `segments`: An array of budget segments, like rows in a spreadsheet. Each segment describes a combination of dimension values and the corresponding budget amount for each year-month.
- `filter`: An optional filter expression to narrow down the scope of the budget based on specific dimension values. This is useful later when generating a budget report, as it allows you to exclude certain line items from the report rather than marking them as "unbudgeted". For example, you might define the budget filter to only include AWS costs, and exclude all Tax line items from the budget.
  
Here's an example budget for "2023 Q1" listing the expected costs for each vendor, for the first three months of the year:
~~~~
{
  "name": "2023 Q1",
  "metric": "cost_amortized_unblended_adj",
  "dimensions": ["vendor"],
  "yearMonths": ["2023-01", "2023-02", "2023-03"],
  "segments": [
    {"dimensionValues": ["AWS"], "budgetAmounts": [100, 110, 120]},
    {"dimensionValues": ["GCP"], "budgetAmounts": [200, 230, 240]}
  ]
}
~~~~

For full details on the budget properties, please refer to the Budget CRUD actions below.

## Budget JSON Editor UI

There is a prototype, standalone tool for editing budget JSON. It provides an interactive UI that enables you to visualize, edit, and validate budget JSON data:

 - [Budget JSON Editor UI](https://s3-us-west-1.amazonaws.com/rs-api-docs/bill_analysis/budget_json_editor/index.html)

Features:

- **Two-way editing**: The editor displays the budget JSON on the left side and an editable UI representation on the right side. Changes made in either view are automatically reflected in the other.
- **Spreadsheet integration**: You can copy the budget table to a spreadsheet or paste content from a spreadsheet, making it easy to convert between formats.
- **Local validation**: The JSON data is validated locally in the browser, ensuring compatibility with the budget API.

## Budget Reports
The API also includes a powerful "Report" action, which allows you to generate a detailed report comparing your budget with actual spend. The report can be filtered by date range, aggregated across dimensions, and even include unbudgeted spend to identify new costs not covered by your existing budget.

For more information, please refer to the description for the `budgets/{id}/report` action, below.

# Rule-Based Dimensions API

## Deprecated
~~~~
This API is deprecated and is no longer being maintained. Please refer to new API documentation found below
~~~~
https://developer.flexera.com/docs/api/finops-customizations/v1

This API lets you create new dimensions in Optima that will be populated according to rules you define.

You can use these new dimensions throughout Optima to look at your costs from new, meaningful perspectives.

A common use case is to create several dimensions like **Department** or **Environment**, populated based on known account values.

You might define a **Department** rule-based dimension with a rule for each known account.
For instance, if the account is "aws-123", then use the value "Finance".
In that way, all the "aws-123" costs will be classified as being in the "Finance" Department. 

## API

The main API route, `/orgs/{org}/settings/rule_based_dimensions`, lets you read/write the entire rule-based dimensions JSON configuration for the org.

There are also two other API routes that let you work with a subset of the config -- a single rule-based dimension, or a single rules list:
  - `/orgs/{org}/settings/rule_based_dimensions/{id}`
  - `/orgs/{org}/settings/rule_based_dimensions/{id}/rules/{effective_at}`

There is a prototype UI where you can paste in JSON on the left and view/edit a human-readable version on the right:
- [Rule-Based Dimension JSON Editor](https://reference.rightscale.com/bill_analysis/rbd_json_editor/full_config.html)

The overall JSON configuration defines all the rule-based dimensions, each one looking like this:
~~~~
{
  "name": "Department",
  "id":   "rbd_department",
  "dated_rules": [
    {
      "effective_at": "2021-01",
      "rules": [...]
    }
  ]
}
~~~~
Each dimension has an `id` and a display `name`.
It also has a `dated_rules` list describing how to populate the dimension over time.

## Rules List

A `rules` list describes how a rule-based dimension should be populated.
A rule simply has a `condition` and a `value`.
As each line of your bill data is being gathered in Optima, the rules will be evaluated in order and the first rule to match will determine the value to populate for that row.

Here's an example rule.
It says: if the vendor account is "12345", populate the rule-based dimension with value "Finance":
~~~~
{
  "condition": {
    "type":      "dimension_equals",
    "dimension": "vendor_account",
    "value":     "12345"
  },
  "value": {
    "text": "Finance"
  }
}
~~~~
If you're populating a dimension based on 100 different accounts, your rules list might have 100 rules just like that one, specifying the value to use for each of the 100 accounts.

### Rule Condition

A rule's condition could be:
 - The `dimension_equals` type
 - A boolean operator type: `and`, `or`, `not` 
 - Empty (null), meaning the rule will match unconditionally

A `dimension_equals` condition checks whether a dimension equals a certain value.
Most of the dimensions in Optima can be referenced:
- Default dimensions:
  - `availability_zone`
  - `bill_entity`
  - `bill_source`
  - `billing_account`
  - `commitment_id`
  - `commitment_name`
  - `database_edition`
  - `database_engine`
  - `deployment_option`
  - `description`
  - `instance_type`
  - `instance_type_family`
  - `invoice_id`
  - `license_model`
  - `line_item_type`
  - `manufacturer_name`
  - `meter_category`
  - `operating_system`
  - `product_order_name`
  - `purchase_option`
  - `region`
  - `resource_group`
  - `resource_type`
  - `service`
  - `service_family`
  - `usage_type`
  - `usage_unit`
  - `vendor`
  - `vendor_account`
  - `vendor_account_name`

- Any custom tag dimensions
- Any other rule-based dimensions (as long as the reference doesn't create a circular dependency among the rule-based dimensions) 

A rule's condition could also be more complex, using the boolean operators `and`, `or`, or `not` to build a larger, nested expression.
For example:

_"vendor is AWS **and** service is EC2":_
~~~~
{
  "type": "and",
  "expressions": [
    {"type":"dimension_equals", "dimension":"vendor",  "value":"AWS"},
    {"type":"dimension_equals", "dimension":"service", "value":"EC2"}
  ]
}
~~~~

_"vendor is **not** Azure":_
~~~~
{
  "type": "not",
  "expression": {
    "type":"dimension_equals", "dimension":"vendor", "value":"Azure"
  }
}
~~~~

Rule conditions must use the underlying cost dimension values, not UI display labels.
Some UI surfaces show friendlier names for display.
For example, the displayed vendor name "Google" may correspond to the underlying vendor value "GCP", which is the value the rule must use.
If a dimension is not offered as a dropdown in the rule editor, inspect your cost data to determine the exact raw values present in your org.

## Rules can change over time
The rules for a rule-based dimension are able to change over time — you could define a fresh rules list for each calendar month, if desired.

The earlier example showed one rules list which takes effect in 2021-January ("2021-01"):
~~~
  "dated_rules": [
    {"effective_at": "2021-01", "rules": [...]}
  ]
~~~
Those rules remain in effect until another rules list is defined for a subsequent month.
For instance, if you have changes starting in the month of April, so you could add a `dated_rules` entry effective "2021-04" with the full `rules` list that you want to be used from that point forward:
~~~
  "dated_rules": [
    {"effective_at": "2021-01", "rules": [...]},
    {"effective_at": "2021-04", "rules": [...<fresh list>...]}
  ]
~~~

## Quotas
An org may define up to 50 rule-based dimensions. And each dimension may define up to 48 rules lists, meaning the rules list can change over time (at 48 unique "effective_at" dates).

A rules list normally supports up to 500 rules.
To limit the complexity of the condition expressions, there may be 1,000 plain condition elements (whether of type "dimension_equals", "and", "or", or "not") used across the entire list after mapping optimization. That means a list might have 500 simple "dimension_equals" rules, or on the other extreme, might only be allowed to have one rule if that rule contains 1,000 condition elements (e.g. a large "or" expression with 999 "dimension_equals" checks). 

### Special Case
There is also a special case on the number of rules: if a list consists of rules that simply check the value of the same dimension (or set of dimensions), we can optimize that and can allow up to 40,000 raw rules in that list, as long as the optimized representation has no more than 500 rule groups.

A common use case would be to populate a rule-based dimension entirely based on the value of the "vendor_account" dimension. 
For instance, you might know the "Department" that should be assigned for every possible account value.
The rules list could support mapping up to 40,000 "vendor_account" values that exist in the org, following this format:
~~~
"rules": [
  {
    "condition": {"type":"dimension_equals", "dimension":"vendor_account", "value":"account_1"},
    "value": {"text":"Finance"}
  },
  {
    "condition": {"type":"dimension_equals", "dimension":"vendor_account", "value":"account_2"},
    "value": {"text":"Engineering"}
  },
  ...<up to 39,998 more rules like the two above>...
]
~~~
This same optimization also applies for rules that check the value of multiple dimensions.
As long as each rule consists of an `and` expression that checks the value of up to 6 dimensions, we can optimize that mapping and support up to 40,000 rules in that list. 
Each of those rules must be checking the same set of dimensions, for example all the rules might check both the "vendor_account" and "resource_group" dimensions.

Across all rule-based dimensions, a single effective month may have up to 400,000 applicable raw rules in total, and up to 2,000 optimized rule groups after mapping optimization.

## Rule-Based Dimension for Billing Center Allocation

This section outlines the use of a special rule-based dimension, `rbd_bc`, as a powerful alternative to traditional [billing center allocation rules](https://docs.flexera.com/flexera/EN/Optima/Allocation_Rules.htm).

### Advantages of `rbd_bc`

Compared to traditional allocation rules, using `rbd_bc` provides the following benefits:
- Enables the rules to change over time, allowing a different rules list for each month.
- Provides the ability to reference other dimensions that are unavailable to traditional allocation rules, such as other rule-based dimensions, custom tag dimensions, and most built-in dimensions.
- Simplifies the allocation process because one rules list directly assigns costs to leaf-node billing centers, whereas traditional allocation rules require separate rules lists at each level of the hierarchy.

### How to Use `rbd_bc`

To use `rbd_bc` for billing center allocation, follow these steps:

1. Create a rule-based dimension `rbd_bc` which will take over assigning billing center allocations.
   - The `id` must be `rbd_bc`.
   - The `name` can be anything, like "BC", or "Assign to BC", etc. Like any other rule-based dimension, it will be visible in the UI.
1. Choose an `effective_at` for the dated rules list. This controls a one-way switchover: starting on that date, the traditional billing center allocation rules will be overridden by this rule-based dimension’s assignments.
1. Write rules to assign costs to a "leaf-node" billing center ID, for example:

       IF vendor_account = "account1" THEN "bc123"

   The end result is that `rbd_bc` will be populated with the ID of the billing center to assign to.
   And the billing center should be a leaf node in the hierarchy, allowing you to freely assign to a billing center several layers down.

#### Example `rbd_bc` Configuration

Here’s an example rule-based dimension configuration which can be pasted into the [prototype editor UI](https://reference.rightscale.com/bill_analysis/rbd_json_editor/full_config.html) for further editing.
It defines an `rbd_bc` with two rules, each assigning an account to a specific billing center:
~~~
{
  "rule_based_dimensions": [
    {
      "id": "rbd_bc",
      "name": "Assign to BC",
      "dated_rules": [
        {
          "effective_at": "2023-01",
          "rules": [
            {
              "condition": {
                "type":      "dimension_equals", 
                "dimension": "vendor_account",
                "value":     "798380790996"
              },
              "value": {"text": "dmsP6WK7qL6yiluIl_3iOQ"}
            },
            {
              "condition": {
                "type":      "dimension_equals", 
                "dimension": "vendor_account",
                "value":     "594348054263"
              },
              "value": {"text": "YbPKQSkO_qoE6hJ8nx9vkg"}
            }
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
~~~
Use the Rule-Based Dimensions API to create the `rbd_bc` dimension.
The next time costs are imported, the billing center assignments will be driven by the `rbd_bc` values, starting on its earliest effective_at date (2023-01 in this example).
The traditional billing center allocation rules will only affect dates before the `rbd_bc` effective_at date.

### `rbd_bc` for Recommendations

The `rbd_bc` dimension will also override billing center allocation on [savings recommendations](https://docs.flexera.com/flexeraone/EN/WhatsNew/FeatureList/CCORecommendations.htm). This works by internally populating the rule-based dimensions (RBDs) on each recommendation and using the `rbd_bc` value to allocate the recommendation to a billing center.

However, recommendations are separate from cost data and only have two fields available for RBD rules to reference:
- `vendor_account`
- `resource_group`

Any RBD rules checking the recommendation's account or resource group should work, for example:
- `IF vendor_account == "A" THEN "bc123"`
- `IF resource_group == "B" THEN "bc456"`

If an RBD rule checks the value of an unsupported dimension, such as `bill_source == "X"`, that clause will evaluate to false because the recommendation doesn't have a `bill_source` field.

But a rule containing an unsupported dimension could still match if it contained an `OR` expression.
Consider the following example rule condition that checks two fields:
```
bill_source == "X" OR vendor_account == "A"
```

Since `bill_source` doesn't exist on recommendations, the `bill_source == "X"` clause evaluates to false. However, the overall rule can still match if `vendor_account == "A"`.

post.description:
Returns a report comparing the budget, forecast to the actual spend.

The response is similar to the rows returned by the `costs/aggregated` API.

Each row represents a specific combination of dimension values and timestamp, 
and includes the corresponding budget amount, forecast amount and actual spend amount.

By default, the report contains one row for each combination of budget segment and year-month. 
For example, for a budget with 10 budget segments covering 12 months, 
the report would return 120 rows (i.e., 10 segments * 12 months).

### Filtering
To narrow the report to a specific range of year-months, specify the start and end dates.
  
### Aggregation across budget segments
The report API can sum up results based on the requested `dimensions`.

For example, consider a budget broken down by two dimensions: Vendor and Account.

- If the `dimensions` list includes both Vendor and Account, the report will display the full budget details, with rows for potentially dozens of accounts.
- If the `dimensions` list includes only Vendor, the report will return fewer rows, providing a summary of the budget and spend for each vendor.
- If the `dimensions` list is empty, the report will return just one row for each year-month, summarizing the total budget and spend across all budget segments.

### Aggregation across year-months

The report API can also sum up results across year-months.

By default, it returns one row for each budget segment and year-month combination.

However, by setting the `summarized` parameter to `true`,
the report will return only one row per budget segment, 
representing its total budget and spend across all the selected year-months.

### Unbudgeted spend
The `includeUnbudgeted` option helps identify new dimension values in the cost data
that were not described by the budget.

For example, a budget may have segments for 10 specific account values. 
By default, the budget report returns rows only for those 10 accounts.

If an 11th account appears in the billing data, it will not be included in the budget report.

Setting the `includeUnbudgeted` parameter to `true` adds rows 
for all other combinations of dimension values found in the cost data, marking them as "unbudgeted".

This allows you to see the unbudgeted spend for the 11th account. You may then wish to either:
- update the budget to include the new account,
- or update the budget filter expression to exclude the account.

post.description:
Queries the costs stored at the given granularity, filtered by the BillingCenterIDs provided. Returns aggregated costs grouped by the specified dimensions.
See also: the `costs/select` action.
For month granularity, the start_at and end_at times are specified in YYYY-MM format, and can cover no more than 24 months. For day granularity, the start_at and end_at times are specified in YYYY-MM-DD format, and can cover no more than 31 days. User must have the 'optima:billing_center:show' privilege on the billing center(s) to make this call.

post.description:
Queries the costs stored at the given granularity, filtered by the BillingCenters provided.
This action is nearly identical to `costs/aggregated` except this returns the stored costs unmodified, with no group-by aggregation performed. So it can quickly return results (up to the max row `limit`) even for queries that would otherwise produce a very large response. Additionally, it supports returning the `resource_id` dimension.
For month granularity, the start_at and end_at times are specified in YYYY-MM format, and can cover no more than 24 months. For day granularity, the start_at and end_at times are specified in YYYY-MM-DD format, and can cover no more than 31 days. User must have the 'optima:billing_center:show' privilege on the billing center(s) to make this call.

build_on_adjustments.description:
If none specified, the base cost is simply the raw cost. 
Can also specify one or more of the adjustment names that were defined earlier in the adjustment list, and the base cost will be the net cost after those adjustments are applied.

rules.description:
List of rules to determine the cost/usage multipliers to apply to a given cost row.
The rules will be evaluated in order until one matches. If none matches, this adjustment is not applied.
The list may contain up to 100 rules.

Adjustment.description:
An adjustment that will be applied to any cost row for which one of the rules match.
The first rule to match will determine the cost & usage multipliers to use.
The base cost will be the raw cost of the row, or if any build_on_adjustments are specified, then those adjusted costs will be added in to form the base cost.
The final cost of this adjustment will be the (base_cost * cost_multiplier) + (usage_amount * usage_multiplier)
